newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: War crimes tribunal on ex-Yugoslavia - key facts.
newsitem.headline: War crimes tribunal on ex-Yugoslavia - key facts.

text.p: Following are the key facts about the U.N. war crimes tribunal for former Yugoslavia.
* The International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia was established by Resolution 827 of the United Nations Security Council in May 1993.
* It is the first international body for the prosecution of war crimes since the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials held in the aftermath of World War Two.
* Resolution 827 stipulates that all states are obliged to cooperate fully with the tribunal.
* The tribunal has jurisdiction over individuals responsible for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity in the territory of the former Yugoslavia after January 1, 1991.
* It has no police force of its own and relies on the former Yugoslav republics, other states or the NATO-led peace Stabilisation Force (SFOR) in Bosnia to make arrests.
* The tribunal consists of two trial chambers, each with three judges, and one appeals chamber with five judges.
* Judge Antonio Cassese of Italy is president of the tribunal. Chief prosecutor Richard Goldstone of South Africa was succeeded on October 1, 1996 by Louise Arbour of Canada.
* The tribunal may not try suspects in absentia, nor impose the death penalty. The maximum sentence is life imprisonment.
* As of July 14, 1997 the tribunal had announced the indictment of 77 suspects, but recent arrests have revealed the existence of a secret list of unpublished indictments.
* The two most prominent suspects indicted by the tribunal are former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic and his military commander, General Ratko Mladic, both of whom remain at large.
* The tribunal currently holds 10 indicted suspects at its 24-cell detention centre in The Hague.

* The tribunal began its first trial, of Bosnian Serb Dusan Tadic, on May 7, 1996. Exactly a year later, Tadic was found guilty of torture and murder of Moslems in and near the Omarska prison camp in 1992.
* On July 14, Tadic was sentenced to 20 years in prison. His lawyers have appealed against the guilty verdict.
